title: The same Lord in all beings
hookLine: an outcaste in a narrow lane asks Shankara a question; chapter thirteen gives the same answer with one sun
carry: the same Lord lives in every being

lines: MOVE WHAT? THE SELF FROM THE SELF?
cards: There's a story told about Shankara, the great teacher of oneness.

In Kashi, coming up from the Ganga, he meets an outcaste man with his dogs in a narrow lane, and Shankara, or in some tellings his students, calls out: move aside. The man doesn't. He asks: move what?
This body made of food, away from that one? Or the self, away from the self? Is the sun shining in the Ganga a different sun from the one in the water of my lane?
Tradition says Shankara bowed to him and called him his teacher. Chapter thirteen ends on the same picture.

teach.b: First, two words. Prakriti: nature, everything that moves and changes, the body, the senses, the mind. Purusha: the person, the conscious one who experiences it.
Verse twenty: nature is behind all doing; the person is behind the experiencing of pleasure and pain. Then verse twenty-seven, the center of today.
The one who sees the supreme Lord standing the same in all beings, not perishing when they perish, truly sees.
Verse twenty-eight follows: samam pashyan, seeing the same Lord everywhere, such a person doesn't harm the self by the self. Commentators unpack that line in more than one way.

Some readers hear in it: if the same one lives in everyone, hurting another is hurting yourself. Verse twenty-nine: the one who sees that nature does the acting, and that the self is not the doer, sees.
Near the end come two pictures.

teach.h: NEVER STAINED. ONE SUN, MANY FIELDS.
teach.b: Verse thirty-two: space is everywhere, and it's so subtle it's never stained by what it holds. So the self in every body is never stained.
Verse thirty-three: as the one sun lights this whole world, the knower of the field lights the whole field. One light, many fields.
The schools differ again on how literally to take the oneness: Advaita as one self, Vaishnava schools as one Lord dwelling in many selves.

teach.h: THE SAME LORD IN ALL BEINGS.
teach.b: Either way, the verse asks for the seeing the man in the lane asked of Shankara: look at anyone, and see the same Lord.

how: Many Hindus greet others with namaste, often explained as honoring the divine in the other person; Gita 13.27–13.28, seeing the same Lord in all beings, is one of the verses teachers point to for this.

o: the same, even: seeing one Lord alike in all beings
treating every person in exactly the same way
calm, an inner peace that nothing can disturb

games.q: the chapter's last pictures — tap the pairs.

s: verse 28 says seeing the same Lord everywhere, you don't harm the self by the self
some readers hear in it: if the same one lives in all, harming another harms yourself.
the Gita says the self in a body gets stained by what the body does
verse 32: like space, it's so subtle it is never stained.
in the story told about Shankara, the outcaste asks whether the self in one body differs from the self in another
move what aside, he asks: the body made of food, or the self from the self?

games.q: Krishna wants one picture for how the knower lights every field. what does he choose?
o: the one sun lighting the whole world.
a river flowing into the sea.
games.why: the one sun. verse 33: as one sun lights this whole world, the knower of the field lights the whole field.

practice: Picture a light at your center, steady and warm, then the same light in the person nearest you, in the next room or the next house.

Widen it: someone across town, someone whose name you'll never know, and, if you're willing, someone you find hard. Greet each one inwardly with namaste, i bow to you. If you pray, add: the same Lord lives in you.
If you don't, simply see the same light. You don't have to like them; just see it.

wordCard.voice: Sama, the same, even. Gita thirteen, twenty-seven: the one who sees the same Lord standing in all beings, imperishable in the perishing, truly sees.

orig.note: Sanskrit: sama, the same, even; in 13.28, 'samam pashyan', seeing the same everywhere.

carryVoice: Your line: the same Lord lives in every being. One sun, in every water. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 13.27–13.29 (seeing the same in all; nature acts)
Manisha Panchakam, traditionally attributed to Shankara (the story of the outcaste at Kashi)
